questions.stem: The ICF volume is 28 litres. The ECF volume is 14 litres. The osmolarity is 300 milliosmoles/litre. The subject loses 2 litres of ECF fluid and each litre has 200 milliosmoles. In such a case, which one of the following will be true?

options.label: C
options.text: ICFV will increase and ECFV will decrease

options.label: D
options.text: ICFV will decrease and ECFV will increase

questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

When a person loses 2 liters of ECF fluid with a concentration of 200 milliosmoles/liter, it constitutes a hypotonic fluid loss (since normal osmolarity is 300 milliosmoles/liter). This leads to the following physiological changes:

 

ECF Volume (ECFV): The direct loss of fluid decreases the ECF volume.

 

ECF Osmolarity: The loss of hypotonic fluid leaves behind a higher concentration of solutes in the ECF, increasing its osmolarity.

 

Water Movement to Maintain Osmotic Balance: To balance the osmotic gradient, water moves out of the ICF into the ECF.

 

This movement reduces the ICF volume (ICFV).

 

Final Outcome:

 

Both the ICF and ECF volumes decrease.

 

Osmolarity increases in both compartments but equalizes between them due to the water shift.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. ICFV and ECFV will increase: Incorrect. Both volumes decrease due to fluid loss and subsequent water redistribution.

 

Option C. ICFV will increase and ECFV will decrease: Incorrect. Water does not move into the ICF; instead, it moves out of the ICF to balance the higher osmolarity in the ECF.

 

Option D. ICFV will decrease and ECFV will increase: Incorrect. While ICF volume decreases, ECF volume also decreases due to the initial fluid loss.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of hypotonic fluid loss from the ECF, water shifts from the ICF to the ECF to restore osmotic equilibrium. Both ICF and ECF volumes decrease, and osmolarity increases in both compartments.

questions.stem: On a return visit after receiving a diagnosis of functional dyspepsia, a 35- year-old woman reports sensations of early satiety and discomfort in the epigastric region after a meal. These symptoms are most likely a result of: ​​​​​​​

options.label: A
options.text: Malfunction of adaptive relaxation in the gastric reservoir

options.label: B
options.text: Elevated frequency of contractions in the antral pump

options.label: D
options.text: Premature onset of the interdigestive phase of gastric motility

questions.answerText: Malfunction of adaptive relaxation in the gastric reservoir
questions.solutionHtml:
n>

 

Explanation:

 

Functional dyspepsia is a common gastrointestinal disorder characterized by symptoms such as early satiety, postprandial fullness, and epigastric discomfort. Among the mechanisms contributing to functional dyspepsia, a malfunction of adaptive relaxation in the gastric reservoir is the most likely cause of early satiety.

 

  • Adaptive Relaxation:
    • The stomach adapts to incoming food by relaxing its muscular tone to accommodate the meal, which is referred to as adaptive relaxation.
    • If this relaxation is impaired, the stomach cannot expand properly, leading to sensations of fullness (early satiety) and discomfort after a meal.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Elevated frequency of contractions in the antral pump: Incorrect. Contractions in the antral pump are responsible for grinding and mixing food, not early satiety or postprandial fullness. Dysregulated contractions could lead to delayed gastric emptying but are not linked to early satiety.

 

Option C. An incompetent lower esophageal sphincter: Incorrect. An incompetent lower esophageal sphincter (LES) results in gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), causing symptoms like heartburn and regurgitation, not early satiety or epigastric discomfort.

 

Option D. Premature onset of the interdigestive phase of gastric motility: Incorrect. The migrating motor complex (MMC) occurs during fasting to clear residual food and debris. Premature MMC onset would cause hunger, not early satiety, and is unrelated to postprandial symptoms.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Early satiety and postprandial discomfort in functional dyspepsia are most likely due to a malfunction of adaptive relaxation in the gastric reservoir, which prevents the stomach from accommodating meals effectively. This is a hallmark feature of postprandial distress syndrome, a subtype of functional dyspepsia.

questions.stem: Solute movement by active transport can be distinguished from solute transport by equilibrating carrier mediated transport because active transport:

options.label: A
options.text: Is saturable at high solute concentration

options.label: B
options.text: Is inhibited by other molecules with structures similar to that of the solute

options.label: C
options.text: Moves the solute against its electrochemical gradient

questions.answerText: Moves the solute against its electrochemical gradient
questions.solutionHtml:
>

 

Explanation:

 

Active transport is a process where solutes are moved against their electrochemical gradient, which requires energy input (e.g., ATP or ion gradients). This is a distinguishing feature of active transport compared to facilitated diffusion or equilibrating carrier-mediated transport, which occur passively along the electrochemical gradient.

 

Note :

 

Differences between Active Transport and Carrier-Mediated Transport (Facilitated Diffusion):

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Is saturable at high solute concentration: Incorrect. Both active transport and facilitated diffusion are saturable because they rely on specific transporters.

 

Option B. Is inhibited by other molecules with structures similar to that of the solute: Incorrect. Both processes can be inhibited by competitive molecules.

 

Option D. Allows movement of polar molecules: Incorrect. Both processes allow polar molecules to move, so this cannot distinguish between them.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The defining feature of active transport is its ability to move solutes against their electrochemical gradient, which sets it apart from carrier-mediated transport like facilitated diffusion, which occurs passively along the gradient.

questions.stem: After secretion of trypsinogen into the duodenum, the enzyme is converted into its active form, trypsin, by which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
g>

 

Explanation:

 

Trypsinogen, the inactive precursor (zymogen) of the enzyme trypsin, is secreted by the pancreas into the duodenum. It is activated into trypsin by the enzyme enteropeptidase (also known as enterokinase), which is secreted by the cells lining the duodenum.

 

Key Roles of Trypsin:

 

  • Once activated, trypsin not only continues the process of protein digestion but also activates other pancreatic zymogens, including:
    • Procarboxypeptidase → Carboxypeptidase
    • Chymotrypsinogen → Chymotrypsin
    • Other trypsinogen molecules (autocatalysis).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Procarboxypeptidase: Incorrect. Procarboxypeptidase is another pancreatic zymogen that is activated by trypsin, not the enzyme that activates trypsinogen.

Option C. Pancreatic lipase: Incorrect. Pancreatic lipase is involved in fat digestion, not protein digestion or enzyme activation.

 

Option D. Chymotrypsin: Incorrect. Chymotrypsin is the active form of the zymogen chymotrypsinogen, which is activated by trypsin, not the enzyme that activates trypsinogen.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The activation of trypsinogen into trypsin is catalyzed by enteropeptidase, a key step in initiating protein digestion in the small intestine.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement is true? ​​​​​​​

options.label: A
options.text: Fluid coming from the descending limb of loop of Henle is hypotonic

options.label: B
options.text: Descending limb of loop of Henle is permeable to solutes

options.label: C
options.text: If clearance of substance is greater than GFR, then tubular secretion must be present

options.label: D
options.text: Clearance of a substance is always less than GFR if there is tubular secretion

questions.answerText: If clearance of substance is greater than GFR, then tubular secretion must be present
questions.solutionHtml:
an style="font-size:14.0pt;">Explanation:

 

Clearance refers to the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per unit time. If the clearance of a substance exceeds the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), it means that the substance must be secreted by the tubules in addition to being filtered. An example is PAH (para-aminohippuric acid), which is both filtered and secreted.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fluid coming from the descending limb of the loop of Henle is hypotonic: Incorrect. The descending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to water but impermeable to solutes. Water is reabsorbed into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, making the fluid in the descending limb hypertonic, not hypotonic.

 

Option B. Descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to solutes: Incorrect. The descending limb is permeable to water only, not solutes. The scending limb, on the other hand, is permeable to solutes but not to water.

 

Option D. Clearance of a substance is always less than GFR if there is tubular secretion: Incorrect. If tubular secretion occurs, the clearance of the substance can exceed the GFR (e.g., PAH). This statement contradicts the mechanics of tubular secretion.

 

Key Concept:

 

  • Tubular Secretion:
    Substances secreted into the tubular lumen increase the amount of substance excreted in the urine, resulting in clearance values greater than the GFR.

 

Educational Objective:

 

If the clearance of a substance is greater than the GFR, this indicates the presence of tubular secretion, as seen with PAH, which is used to measure renal plasma flow.

questions.stem: Which one of the following membrane has highest content of protein content per gram of tissue
questions.solutionHtml:
ial membrane

 

Explanation:

 

The inner mitochondrial membrane is known to have the highest protein content per gram of tissue among the given options. This is because proteins play a crucial role in its primary function, which includes electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation. The high protein-to-lipid ratio of the inner mitochondrial membrane reflects the abundance of enzyme complexes and carrier proteins essential for energy metabolism.

 

  • Proteins are heavier and denser than lipids, and the inner mitochondrial membrane is densely packed with functional proteins necessary for its role in cellular respiration.

 

Additionally, when comparing the protein-to-lipid ratio across membranes, the inner mitochondrial membrane consistently ranks the highest due to its specialized role in energy production.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Outer mitochondrial membrane: The outer mitochondrial membrane contains a lower protein-to-lipid ratio than the inner mitochondrial membrane. It primarily acts as a barrier and regulates the entry and exit of molecules, requiring fewer proteins.

 

Option B. Myelin sheath: The myelin sheath has a high lipid content compared to protein, as its primary function is to insulate axons and speed up electrical transmission. This makes it unsuitable for processes requiring high protein content.

 

Option D. Plasma membrane: The plasma membrane has a balanced protein-to-lipid ratio, but it is not as protein-dense as the inner mitochondrial membrane. It plays diverse roles in cell communication, transport, and protection, but these do not demand as many proteins as the inner mitochondrial membrane.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The inner mitochondrial membrane has the highest protein content per gram of tissue, reflecting its critical role in cellular energy metabolism.

questions.stem: Identify the correct statement amongst the following

options.label: A
options.text: Female has less body water content due to more bone mass

options.label: B
options.text: Male has more body water content due to more fat

options.label: C
options.text: Infant has more body water content due to high bone mass

questions.answerText: Infant has more body water content due to less fat
questions.solutionHtml:
>

 

Explanation:

 

Water content in the body is inversely proportional to fat content. Infants have a higher body water percentage compared to adults because their bodies contain relatively less fat. Bone mass is not the determining factor for water content in infants, as their skeletal systems are still developing and are not as dense as those of adults.

 

Key Points:

 

  • Fat is hydrophobic and reduces water content in the body.
  • Infants, having a lower fat content, exhibit a higher proportion of water in their bodies, typically around 70-75%.

 

Thus, the correct statement reflects the fact that infants’ lower fat content is the primary reason for their higher body water percentage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Female has less body water content due to more bone mass: Incorrect. Females generally have less body water content due to a higher fat percentage, not due to bone mass.

 

Option B. Male has more body water content due to more fat: Incorrect. Males typically have more body water content due to lower fat percentage, not higher fat.

 

Option C. Infant has more body water content due to high bone mass: Incorrect. Bone mass in infants is still developing and is not a significant factor in determining body water content.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Infants have the highest body water content among age groups because they have a relatively low fat content, and fat is inversely related to body water percentage.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents the basis for transduction of a sensory stimulus into nerve impulses?

options.label: A
options.text: Change in the ion permeability of the receptor membrane

questions.answerText: Change in the ion permeability of the receptor membrane
questions.solutionHtml:
g>

 

Explanation:

 

Sensory transduction is the process of converting a sensory stimulus into an electrical signal that the nervous system can interpret. This process begins with changes in the ion permeability of the receptor membrane.

 

When a sensory stimulus (e.g., light, sound, or pressure) interacts with the receptor, it alters the receptor membrane's ion permeability, leading to the generation of a graded or receptor potential. This change in ion permeability is the basis for the initial electrical response, which can then be transmitted as a nerve impulse or action potential in downstream cells, such as ganglion cells.

 

For example:

 

  • In photoreceptors, light induces a change in ion channels, modifying ion flow across the receptor membrane.
  • In mechanoreceptors, mechanical pressure alters ion channel permeability.

 

Thus, the initial transduction mechanism relies on changes in ion permeability rather than the generation of an action potential, which is a secondary event in neural communication.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Generation of an action potential: Incorrect. While action potentials are critical for propagating information through the nervous system, they occur after transduction. Not all sensory cells directly generate action potentials; some, like photoreceptors, produce local potentials.

 

Option C. Inactivation of a G-protein–mediated response: Incorrect. G-protein-mediated signaling can play a role in sensory transduction (e.g., in phototransduction), but its inactivation is not a universal basis for transduction. The primary mechanism involves changes in ion permeability.

 

Option D. Protein synthesis: Incorrect. Protein synthesis is not directly involved in the process of sensory transduction. It occurs later as part of cellular responses to stimuli or adaptations.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The basis of sensory transduction lies in the change in the ion permeability of the receptor membrane, allowing the conversion of various forms of energy into electrical signals that the nervous system can process.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is not used for measurement of corresponding body fluid volume?

options.label: C
options.text: Evan’s Blue dye for plasma volume

questions.solutionHtml:
lume

 

Explanation:

 

Body fluid compartments are measured using specific markers that can uniquely identify and quantify different components such as total body water, extracellular fluid, plasma volume, or blood volume. 

 

125I-Albumin:

 

  • Measures plasma volume (not blood volume). For accurate measurement of blood volume, you must account for both plasma and red blood cell content. This is achieved using markers such as chromium-51 labelled RBCs or iron-59 labelled RBCs, not 125I-Albumin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Antipyrine for total body water: Correct. Antipyrine is appropriate for measuring total body water due to its distribution across all compartments.

 

Option B. Inulin for extracellular fluid: Correct. Inulin is a reliable marker for extracellular fluid because it does not penetrate cell membranes.

 

Option C. Evan’s Blue dye for plasma volume: Correct. Evan’s Blue dye binds to plasma proteins and is used specifically for measuring plasma volume.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Blood volume is measured by labeling red blood cells using isotopes like chromium-51 or iron-59. 125I-Albumin is used for measuring plasma volume, not blood volume.

questions.stem: A graphical representation of body fluid and osmolarity was taken of a subject while exercising which led to sweating. Which type of Body fluid disturbance can be seen in given scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
id loss

 

Explanation:

 

Sweating causes the body to lose both water and electrolytes (mainly sodium and chloride). However, the loss of solutes (primarily sodium and chloride) is disproportionate compared to water loss, especially under conditions like cystic fibrosis or during prolonged exercise. In such cases, more solutes are lost relative to water, leading to a decrease in osmolarity of the body fluids, known as hypoosmotic fluid loss.

 

Key Points:

 

  1. Hypoosmotic Nature of Sweat: Sweat is generally hypoosmotic compared to plasma, meaning that it contains relatively fewer solutes compared to water. Prolonged sweating disproportionately reduces solute concentration in the extracellular fluid.
  2. Effect on Body Fluid Osmolarity: This results in hypoosmotic fluid loss, which can decrease the osmolarity of the remaining body fluids.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Isosmotic fluid loss: Incorrect. Isosmotic fluid loss refers to equal loss of water and solutes, as seen in certain types of diarrhea or blood loss. Sweating is not isosmotic.

 

Option C. Hyperosmotic fluid loss: Incorrect. Hyperosmotic fluid loss occurs when water loss exceeds solute loss, causing increased osmolarity in the remaining fluid. This is not typical in sweating, where solute loss is prominent.

 

Option D. Hypoosmotic fluid gain: Incorrect. Hypoosmotic fluid gain would occur when excess water is added to the body, such as with overhydration or excessive hypotonic fluid intake. Sweating results in fluid loss, not gain.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sweating causes hypoosmotic fluid loss, as the body loses more solutes (sodium and chloride) relative to water, particularly under prolonged sweating conditions.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure presents to the emergency department with complaints of progressive shortness of breath and fatigue. His medications include furosemide, enalapril, and spironolactone. Laboratory tests show a serum sodium concentration of 125 mmol/L and a serum potassium coancentration of 5.0 mmol/L. Using the Darrow-Yannet diagram, which of the following best represents his fluid and electrolyte status (Dotted line representing normal condition)?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D)

 

 

 

Explanation:

 

This patient's clinical presentation, medications, and lab findings indicate hypoosmotic fluid loss, as follows:

 

  1. Medications (Diuretics):
    • Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits sodium-potassium-chloride transport in the thick ascending loop of Henle, causing loss of sodium, potassium, and chloride along with water.
    • This excessive sodium and solute loss reduces extracellular fluid (ECF) osmolarity.
  2. Serum Sodium (125 mmol/L):
    • A significantly low serum sodium indicates that the patient is experiencing a loss of hypertonic fluid, where solute loss is more significant than water loss.
  3. Fluid Movement (ECF to ICF):
    • As solutes are lost from the ECF, the osmolarity of the ECF decreases. This creates an osmotic gradient that causes water to move from the ECF into the intracellular fluid (ICF) to restore osmotic equilibrium.
  4. Changes in Volume and Osmolarity:
    • ECF: Osmolarity decreases, and the volume decreases due to fluid loss.
    • ICF: Volume increases as water shifts into cells to achieve osmotic balance.

 

These changes are best depicted in Darrow-Yannet Diagram D, where the ECF volume decreases, osmolarity decreases, and the ICF volume increases.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Isosmotic fluid loss: Incorrect. Isosmotic loss (e.g., hemorrhage or certain diarrhea cases) involves the equal loss of water and solutes, leading to no osmolarity change in either ECF or ICF.

 

Option B. Hypoosmotic fluid loss: Incorrect. The patient is not losing hypoosmotic fluid but experiencing hypoosmotic conditions due to hypertonic fluid loss.

 

Option C. Hyperosmotic fluid loss: Incorrect. Hyperosmotic loss occurs when water loss exceeds solute loss, leading to increased osmolarity. This does not match the findings of this patient with significant sodium depletion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The patient is experiencing hypoosmotic fluid loss, characterized by a decrease in ECF osmolarity, movement of water from ECF to ICF, and a subsequent increase in ICF volume. This is accurately represented in Darrow-Yannet Diagram D.

questions.stem: In a patient with malignant hyperthermia triggered by anesthesia, which of the following alterations in the process of excitation-contraction (EC) coupling is primarily responsible for the rapid onset of muscle rigidity and hyperthermia?

options.label: A
options.text: Inactivity of L-type calcium channels in the sarcolemma

options.label: B
options.text: Overactivity of calcium channels ryanodine receptors (RyR) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)

options.label: C
options.text: Impaired release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: D
options.text: Reduced activity of voltage-gated sodium channels in the muscle membrane

questions.answerText: Overactivity of calcium channels ryanodine receptors (RyR) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Malignant hyperthermia is a life-threatening condition triggered by certain anesthetics (e.g., succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics) in genetically predisposed individuals. It is primarily caused by a mutation in the RYR1 (ryanodine receptor 1) gene, which regulates calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) in skeletal muscle cells.

 

  1. Overactive Ryanodine Receptors (RYR1):
    • The RYR1 mutation causes overactivity of calcium release channels in the SR.
    • Upon exposure to a triggering agent, these receptors release excessive calcium into the myoplasm, even in response to sub-threshold stimuli.
  2. Effects of Excess Calcium:
    • Increased Muscle Contraction: Elevated intracellular calcium levels lead to sustained and excessive muscle contractions, which manifest as muscle rigidity.
    • Heat Generation: Muscle contractions consume ATP, which generates heat. The excessive calcium cycling and ATP consumption result in hyperthermia.
    • Energy Depletion and Acidosis: The metabolic activity overwhelms the muscle’s energy supply, causing lactic acidosis and further worsening the condition.
  3. Treatment:
    • Dantrolene is the treatment of choice. It inhibits the RYR1 receptor, reducing calcium release and alleviating muscle rigidity and hyperthermia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Inactivity of L-type calcium channels in the sarcolemma: Incorrect. L-type calcium channels (dihydropyridine receptors) are involved in initiating calcium release from the SR but are not primarily responsible for malignant hyperthermia. This condition is due to excessive calcium release from RYR1 channels in the SR.

 

Option C. Impaired release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction: Incorrect. Malignant hyperthermia is not related to impaired acetylcholine release. Acetylcholine functions in neuromuscular signaling, and its release remains normal in this condition.

 

Option D. Reduced activity of voltage-gated sodium channels in the muscle membrane: Incorrect. Voltage-gated sodium channels regulate action potential propagation but are not the cause of the excessive calcium release seen in malignant hyperthermia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Malignant hyperthermia is primarily caused by overactivity of ryanodine receptors (RYR1) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to excessive calcium release, sustained muscle contraction, and heat generation. This explains the rapid onset of muscle rigidity and hyperthermia. Dantrolene is the treatment of choice for this condition.

Explanation:

 

Neutral substances, particularly non-polar molecules like gases (e.g., oxygen, carbon dioxide), can freely cross the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane through simple diffusion. This process does not require specific transport proteins or energy and occurs due to the natural movement of molecules down their concentration gradient.

 

  1. Diffusion:
    • It is a passive process where molecules move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
    • Non-polar and neutral molecules do not require any transport mechanisms (like porins or channels) because they can dissolve in the hydrophobic core of the lipid bilayer.
  2. Examples of Molecules Transported via Diffusion:
    • Gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide.
    • Small non-polar molecules like nitrogen gas.
    • Lipid-soluble substances.

 

Other transport mechanisms (porins, ionophores, and channels) are specifically used for polar or charged molecules that cannot easily pass through the lipid bilayer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Porins: Incorrect. Porins are specific channels in the outer membranes of certain cells (e.g., bacteria or mitochondria) that facilitate the transport of hydrophilic molecules, not neutral non-polar substances.

 

Option B. Ionophore: Incorrect. Ionophores are molecules that transport ions across the membrane, not neutral substances. They specifically assist in the transport of charged particles like calcium or potassium.

 

Option C. Channels: Incorrect. Channels are specific protein structures that transport ions or polar molecules, not neutral non-polar substances.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neutral and non-polar substances like gases cross the cell membrane through simple diffusion, a passive process that does not require transport proteins or energy.

le="font-size:14.0pt;">Explanation:

 

The extracellular fluid (ECF) volume can be calculated using the formula:

The absolute refractory period is a phase during which a nerve cannot be stimulated, regardless of the strength of the stimulus. This occurs because the sodium (Na⁺) channels are either already open or in an inactivated state, making it impossible to generate another action potential.

 

This is true and is a defining characteristic of the absolute refractory period.

This is correct and directly explains why a second action potential cannot be initiated during the absolute refractory period.

Thus, both the assertion and reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation for the assertion.

questions.stem: Where do afferent fibers from baroreceptors primarily project for blood pressure control?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Baroreceptors, located in the walls of major blood vessels such as the carotid sinus and aortic arch, detect changes in blood pressure and relay this information to the brainstem for regulation of cardiovascular activity. The afferent fibers of these baroreceptors travel via the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) and the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) and primarily project to the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS) in the medulla.

 

  1. Role of NTS:
    • The NTS is the primary processing center for baroreceptor input in the brainstem.
    • It integrates signals from baroreceptors and sends output to other nuclei involved in cardiovascular regulation, such as:
      • The Cardioinhibitory Center (CIC) located in the Nucleus Ambiguus.
      • The Caudal Ventrolateral Medulla (CVLM), which inhibits the Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla (RVLM) to decrease sympathetic activity and reduce blood pressure.
  2. Stepwise Pathway:
    • Baroreceptor Afferents → NTS → Processed signals modulate activity in:
      • Nucleus Ambiguus (parasympathetic stimulation to decrease heart rate).
      • CVLM and RVLM (adjust sympathetic tone).
  3. Why NTS is Primary:
    • All baroreceptor afferent inputs are first processed in the NTS, making it the central hub for blood pressure regulation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nucleus Ambiguus: Incorrect. The Nucleus Ambiguus is involved in parasympathetic control (via the vagus nerve), but it receives input after signals are processed by the NTS.

 

Option B. Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla (RVLM): Incorrect. The RVLM regulates sympathetic output but is downstream in the pathway and receives inhibitory input from the CVLM, which is influenced by the NTS.

 

Option D. Caudal Ventrolateral Medulla (CVLM): Incorrect. The CVLM is part of the pathway for reducing sympathetic tone, but it receives input from the NTS, not directly from baroreceptors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Afferent fibers from baroreceptors primarily project to the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS) in the medulla, which serves as the primary processing center for blood pressure control.

questions.solutionHtml:
p> 

Explanation:

 

The ventricular action potential consists of five distinct phases (Phases 0–4), each characterized by specific ion movements. 

 

Matching Each Step:

 

  1. Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels (Phase 0):
    1. This marks the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential.
    2. Voltage-gated sodium channels open, allowing Na⁺ to rush into the cell.
    3. C corresponds to Phase 0 (C-4).
  2. Transient outward flow of potassium (Phase 1):
    1. After the initial depolarization, there is a brief transient outward flow of potassium, causing a small repolarization.
    2. This creates the small downward curve seen immediately after Phase 0.
    3. D corresponds to Phase 1 (D-1).
  3. Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels (Phase 2):
    1. This is the plateau phase, where voltage-gated calcium channels open, allowing Ca²⁺ influx. This sustains the action potential and opposes the repolarizing effects of potassium.
    2. A corresponds to Phase 2 (A-2).
  4. Repolarizing potassium currents (Phase 3):
    1. In this phase, potassium channels open, allowing K⁺ to leave the cell, leading to repolarization.
    2. B corresponds to Phase 3 (B-3).
  5. Leaky sodium channels (No role in ventricular action potential):
    1. Leaky sodium channels (funny channels) are not involved in the ventricular action potential. They are characteristic of nodal tissue.
    2. E has no role in ventricular action potential (E-5).

 

Educational Objective:

 

The ventricular action potential progresses through distinct phases (0–4), each driven by specific ion channel activity. Understanding the role of each phase is critical in interpreting cardiac electrophysiology.

 

  • A-2 (Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels in Phase 2)
  • B-3 (Repolarizing K⁺ currents in Phase 3)
  • C-4 (Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels in Phase 0)
  • D-1 (Transient outward flow of potassium in Phase 1)
  • E-5 (Leaky sodium channels have no role)

questions.stemHtml: In a patient, the hypothalamic thermostat was reset from point V to point X as shown below. Which of the following happens in stage Y compared to stage W?
questions.solutionHtml:
eating

 

Explanation:

 

The graph represents the changes in body temperature in response to hypothalamic thermostat resetting, such as in fever. Let's break this down into stages:

 

Stage W (Fever Onset):

  • The hypothalamic thermostat resets to a higher set point (from V to X).
  • To reach the new set point, the body increases its temperature through shivering and other heat-generating mechanisms (e.g., chemical thermogenesis).
  • Vasoconstriction reduces heat loss to the environment, helping to increase body temperature.

 

Stage Y (Resolution of Fever):

  • The hypothalamic thermostat resets back to the normal set point (V).
  • The body temperature is now higher than the set point, and the body must lose heat to restore equilibrium.
  • To achieve this, the body initiates mechanisms to reduce body temperature, including:

 

Sweating: Promotes heat loss via evaporation.

 

Increased blood flow to skin (vasodilation): Facilitates heat dissipation.

 

In stage Y, sweating is the dominant process to decrease body temperature, making it the correct answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Shivering: Incorrect. Shivering occurs during stage W when the body is trying to raise its temperature to match the new set point. It does not occur during stage Y.

 

Option C. Increased blood flow to skin: Partially correct but not the primary mechanism. While vasodilation occurs during stage Y, sweating is the most important mechanism for heat loss in this context.

 

Option D. Inhibition of chemical thermogenesis: Incorrect. Chemical thermogenesis is suppressed when the body is cooling, but this is not a primary mechanism for heat loss in stage Y.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In stage Y (resolution of fever), the hypothalamic thermostat resets to a lower set point, prompting mechanisms like sweating to decrease body temperature and restore homeostasis.

The emergency team, suspecting a potential reflex activation due to an unknown compound in the supplement, reminiscent of the effects seen with Veratrum alkaloids, which one of the following is true regarding the same reflex?

options.label: A
options.text: Activation of carotid body chemoreceptors leads to the reflex condition.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

-size:14.0pt;">Explanation:

 

The clinical scenario describes a reflex similar to the Bezold-Jarisch reflex, which involves:

 

  1. Hypotension
  2. Bradycardia
  3. Apnea

 

This reflex is triggered by chemical or mechanical stimulation of left ventricular receptors in response to certain stimuli, including Veratrum alkaloids or similar compounds. These receptors are part of unmyelinated vagal afferent fibers. Once activated, they trigger a parasympathetic (vagal) response, leading to the observed triad of effects.

 

Key Steps in the Reflex:

 

  1. Stimulation of Left Ventricular Receptors:
    • Veratrum alkaloids or similar compounds activate stretch or chemical-sensitive receptors in the left ventricle.
    • This triggers vagal afferents leading to parasympathetic dominance.
  2. Effects of the Reflex:
    • Bradycardia: Due to increased parasympathetic outflow to the heart.
    • Hypotension: Caused by peripheral vasodilation mediated through vagal stimulation.
    • Apnea: A secondary component of the reflex.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Activation of carotid body chemoreceptors leads to the reflex condition: Incorrect. Carotid body chemoreceptors respond to changes in blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH, not to chemical or stretch stimulation in the left ventricle. This reflex is unrelated to carotid chemoreceptors.

 

Option B. Stimulation of aortic arch stretch receptors induces the reflex: Incorrect. Aortic arch stretch receptors are baroreceptors that respond to changes in blood pressure, not to chemical stimuli like Veratrum alkaloids.

 

Option D. Peripheral vasodilation by direct action on vascular smooth muscle initiates the reflex: Incorrect. Vasodilation is a result of the reflex, not the initiating event. The trigger is the stimulation of left ventricular receptors, not a direct action on vascular smooth muscle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Bezold-Jarisch reflex is triggered by chemical or mechanical stimulation of left ventricular receptors, leading to the triad of bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea. It is mediated through vagal afferents and parasympathetic activation.

questions.stemHtml: Which curve among the following represents the production of Beta-globin chains?
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>curve

 

 

Explanation:

 

The graph depicts the synthesis of different globin chains during development, both in the fetal stage and the postnatal stage, associated with hemoglobin production.

 

Key Points About the Globin Chains:

 

Alpha (Red Curve):

 

The alpha-globin chains are produced continuously starting from the embryonic stage, throughout fetal life, and into adulthood. This is represented by the red curve, which remains stable.

 

Beta (Green Curve):

 

Beta-globin chains are absent or produced in minimal amounts during the fetal stage. After birth, their production increases rapidly, replacing gamma-globin chains to form adult hemoglobin (HbA, alpha-2 beta-2).

 

This increase in beta-globin chain synthesis after birth is represented by the green curve.

 

Gamma (Yellow Curve):

 

The gamma-globin chains are predominant in fetal hemoglobin (HbF, alpha-2 gamma-2). Their production decreases significantly after birth as the transition to adult hemoglobin occurs.

 

Delta (Purple Curve):

 

The delta-globin chains are a minor component of adult hemoglobin, forming HbA2 (alpha-2 delta-2), which constitutes less than 2.5% of total hemoglobin in normal adults. This is represented by the purple curve, which remains at low levels.

 

Conclusion:

 

The green curve represents the production of beta-globin chains, which begins to rise significantly after birth and replaces gamma-globin in forming adult hemoglobin.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The green curve in the graph represents the beta-globin chain synthesis, which starts increasing rapidly after birth to form adult hemoglobin (HbA).

questions.stem: Which of the following increases in COPD? 1. FRC2. TLC3. VC4. FEV1/FVC
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is characterized by air trapping and reduced expiratory airflow, which leads to changes in lung volumes and capacities. Here's how the different parameters are affected:

 

  1. FRC (Functional Residual Capacity):
    • FRC is the sum of Residual Volume (RV) and Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV).
    • In COPD, air trapping increases the RV significantly, which also increases the FRC.
    • FRC increases in COPD.
  2. TLC (Total Lung Capacity):
    • TLC is the total volume of air in the lungs after maximum inspiration, which includes RV, ERV, Tidal Volume (TV), and Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV).
    • In COPD, due to air trapping and hyperinflation, the RV increases, causing an overall increase in TLC.
    • TLC increases in COPD.
  3. VC (Vital Capacity):
    • VC is the total volume of air exhaled after a maximum inspiration, calculated as TLC - RV.
    • While TLC increases in COPD, the increase in RV reduces the amount of air that can be expelled, leading to a normal or decreased VC.
    • VC does not increase in COPD.
  4. FEV1/FVC (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second / Forced Vital Capacity):
    • This ratio decreases in COPD because FEV1 (volume of air forcibly exhaled in the first second) is reduced much more than FVC due to airflow obstruction.
    • FEV1/FVC decreases in COPD.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In COPD, Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) and Total Lung Capacity (TLC) increase due to air trapping and hyperinflation, while FEV1/FVC decreases, and VC remains normal or decreases.

options.label: B
options.text: Defined as the change in pressure per unit change in volume.

options.label: C
options.text: Slightly greater when measured during deflation than when measured during inflation

questions.answerText: Slightly greater when measured during deflation than when measured during inflation
questions.solutionHtml:
ize:14.0pt;">Explanation:

 

Pulmonary compliance refers to the stretchability or distensibility of the lungs and is defined as the change in lung volume per unit change in pressure:

 

Compliance=ΔV/ΔP

 

Compliance is influenced by lung tissue elasticity, alveolar surface tension, and chest wall mechanics. 

 

 This phenomenon is due to hysteresis, a property of lung compliance. During deflation, surfactant lowers surface tension, making deflation easier and compliance slightly greater. During inflation, surface tension in alveoli increases, requiring more pressure for volume expansion

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decreased in emphysema: Incorrect. Compliance is increased in emphysema because of the destruction of elastic fibers in the lung parenchyma. This reduces the lung's ability to recoil, leading to increased distensibility and compliance.

 

Option B. Defined as the change in pressure per unit change in volume: Incorrect. This is the inverse of the definition of compliance. The correct formula is change in volume per unit change in pressure (ΔV/ΔP).

 

Option D. Increased by pulmonary fibrosis: Incorrect. Pulmonary compliance is decreased in pulmonary fibrosis because of the stiffening and scarring of lung tissue, which reduces distensibility.

 

Note:

 

  • Compliance and Diseases:
    • Increased compliance: Emphysema, old age, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
    • Decreased compliance: Pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, and other restrictive lung diseases.
  • Hysteresis in Compliance:
    • Compliance is higher during deflation due to surfactant reducing alveolar surface tension and assisting with easier lung deflation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pulmonary compliance is slightly greater during deflation than inflation due to hysteresis caused by surfactant action. It is increased in emphysema and decreased in pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: In a patient with chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, it is important to understand the role of specific stomach cells. Which factor is primarily associated with enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells of the stomach, and how does it contribute to the patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Histamine, which stimulates gastric acid production, potentially exacerbating ulcer symptoms.

options.label: B
options.text: Gastrin, which promotes mucus production and provides protection against ulcers.

options.label: C
options.text: Pepsinogen, an enzyme involved in protein digestion within the stomach.

options.label: D
options.text: Secretin, a hormone that regulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, influencing digestion.

questions.answerText: Histamine, which stimulates gastric acid production, potentially exacerbating ulcer symptoms.
questions.solutionHtml:
p>

 

Explanation:

 

Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the stomach play a crucial role in the regulation of gastric acid secretion. These cells release histamine, which acts on H2 receptors on parietal cells, stimulating the secretion of hydrochloric acid (HCl). In conditions like chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, overproduction of histamine can lead to excessive acid secretion, exacerbating symptoms and impeding ulcer healing.

 

The release of histamine by ECL cells is primarily regulated by gastrin (released by G cells) and inhibited by somatostatin (released by D cells). The interplay of these factors is critical for maintaining gastric homeostasis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Gastrin: Gastrin is secreted by G cells in the stomach, not ECL cells. While it stimulates ECL cells to release histamine, it does not directly contribute to mucus production or ulcer protection. Gastrin's primary function is to enhance acid secretion indirectly.

 

Option C. Pepsinogen: Pepsinogen is secreted by chief cells, not ECL cells. It is a precursor of pepsin, which aids in protein digestion. It has no direct role in the histamine-mediated regulation of gastric acid production.

 

Option D. Secretin: Secretin is a hormone released by the small intestine, specifically the duodenum, in response to acidic chyme. It primarily influences pancreatic enzyme and bicarbonate secretion, not gastric acid secretion or histamine release.

 

Educational Objective:

 

ECL cells in the stomach release histamine, which stimulates gastric acid secretion via H2 receptors on parietal cells. This mechanism is significant in the pathophysiology of conditions like chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

It is due to an increase in ventricular pressure caused by the filling of blood during diastole. An image is provided below that further supplements the findings stated above. Explanation:

 

Frank-Starling’s law describes the relationship between ventricular preload (the stretch of cardiac muscle fibers due to blood filling during diastole) and stroke volume (the amount of blood pumped out of the ventricle during systole). According to this principle, an increase in ventricular preload results in greater stretch of the myocardial fibers, which in turn leads to a more forceful contraction and an increased stroke volume, up to a physiological limit.

 

The graph demonstrates this concept:

 

  • In the preload-dependent zone, stroke volume increases with rising ventricular preload, indicative of a patient responsive to volume expansion.
  • In the preload-independent zone, stroke volume plateaus despite further increases in preload, indicating a non-responsive patient.

 

This law is fundamental to understanding cardiac physiology and hemodynamic monitoring.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vascular hyalinosis: Vascular hyalinosis refers to a pathological process involving the accumulation of hyaline material in small blood vessels, often associated with conditions like hypertension or diabetes. It does not describe the preload-stroke volume relationship depicted in the graph.

Option D. Vascular resistance: Vascular resistance is a measure of the resistance offered by blood vessels to blood flow, determined by vessel diameter and blood viscosity. It is unrelated to the preload and stroke volume concepts illustrated in the graph.

Frank-Starling’s law states that the stroke volume of the heart increases in response to an increase in the volume of blood filling the heart (preload), up to a physiological limit, as depicted in the graph.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man visits his doctor because his wife has long complained of his snoring. He undergoes polysomnography and ventilatory response testing to ascertain the extent and cause of his sleep apnea. The activity of the central chemoreceptors is stimulated by which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in the metabolic rate of the surrounding brain tissue

options.label: B
options.text: A decrease in the PO2 of blood flowing through the brain

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in the pH of the CSF

questions.answerText: An increase in the PCO2 of blood flowing through the brain
questions.solutionHtml:
;

 

Explanation:

 

Central chemoreceptors are located in the medulla oblongata and are responsible for detecting changes in the chemical composition of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Their primary stimulus is an increase in PCO2 (partial pressure of carbon dioxide) in the blood flowing through the brain. When PCO2 rises, carbon dioxide diffuses into the CSF and combines with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogen ions (H⁺) and bicarbonate. The resulting increase in H⁺ concentration (lower pH) in the CSF stimulates the central chemoreceptors to enhance respiratory drive, aiming to expel CO2 and restore homeostasis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A decrease in the metabolic rate of the surrounding brain tissue: A decrease in metabolic rate reduces CO2 production and acid formation, thereby lowering the stimulus for central chemoreceptors. This does not stimulate central chemoreceptor activity.

 

Option B. A decrease in the PO2 of blood flowing through the brain: A decrease in oxygen levels primarily stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors located in the carotid and aortic bodies, not central chemoreceptors.

 

Option D. An increase in the pH of the CSF: An increase in pH reflects alkalosis, which would reduce respiratory drive and inhibit central chemoreceptor activity. Central chemoreceptors are instead stimulated by a decrease in pH (acidosis) caused by increased PCO2 levels.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Central chemoreceptors are stimulated by an increase in PCO2 in the blood, leading to acidification of the CSF and enhanced respiratory drive to expel CO2. Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to low PO2 levels, not central ones.

Central chemoreceptors are instead stimulated by a decrease in pH (acidosis) caused by increased PCO2 levels. Educational Objective: Central chemoreceptors are stimulated by an increase in PCO2 in the blood, leading to acidification of the CSF and enhanced respiratory drive to expel CO2. Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to low PO2 levels, not central ones.

questions.stem: A 53 year old male is brought to the emergency department with complains of right sided weakness and jargon speech. A CT brain was ordered to rule out haemorrhagic stroke. On neurological examination, there is normal object recognition but loss of comprehension. Which of the following areas is affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
yrus

 

Explanation:

 

The superior temporal gyrus is a critical area of the brain that contains Wernicke's area, which is primarily responsible for language comprehension. Damage to this area results in Wernicke’s aphasia, characterized by fluent but nonsensical speech (jargon speech) and impaired comprehension.

 

In this patient:

 

  • Jargon speech indicates that the patient can speak fluently but the speech lacks meaning, consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia.
  • Normal object recognition suggests that the inferior temporal lobe, responsible for visual object recognition, is unaffected.
  • Loss of comprehension aligns with dysfunction in Wernicke's area, located in the superior temporal gyrus, typically in the dominant hemisphere (left for most individuals).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inferior frontal gyrus: The inferior frontal gyrus houses Broca's area, which is responsible for speech production. Damage to Broca's area causes Broca’s aphasia, characterized by non-fluent speech but preserved comprehension, which is not consistent with this patient’s presentation.

 

Option C. Arcuate fasciculus: The arcuate fasciculus is a white matter tract connecting Broca’s area (speech production) and Wernicke’s area (language comprehension). Damage to this structure results in conduction aphasia, characterized by intact comprehension and fluent speech but impaired repetition. This is not the case here.

 

Option D. Both A & B: Damage to both Wernicke's area (in the superior temporal gyrus) and Broca's area (in the inferior frontal gyrus) would result in global aphasia, where both speech production and comprehension are severely impaired. The patient in this scenario does not exhibit these features.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Damage to Wernicke’s area, located in the superior temporal gyrus, causes Wernicke’s aphasia, characterized by fluent but nonsensical speech and impaired comprehension, with normal object recognition.

questions.stem: In a patient presenting with a suspected gastrointestinal motility disorder, an endoscopic biopsy reveals alterations of Dense bodies in smooth muscle tissue. Which structural feature found at a specific site within smooth muscle cells is associated with the attachment of actin filaments and contributes to the contractile function. This altered structure is analogous to which structure found in skeletal muscle? ​​​​​​​
questions.solutionHtml:
. B) Z line 

 

Explanation:

 

In smooth muscle cells, dense bodies serve as anchoring points for actin filaments, playing a critical role in the contractile function of the muscle. These dense bodies are scattered throughout the cytoplasm and attached to the sarcolemma, facilitating contraction by anchoring the contractile proteins.

 

 

In skeletal muscle, the analogous structure to dense bodies is the Z line (or Z disc). Z lines are the structural sites within the sarcomere where actin filaments attach, marking the boundaries of each sarcomere. Both structures serve a similar function of anchoring actin filaments, though the organization of contractile proteins is less regular in smooth muscle compared to skeletal muscle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A band: The A band in skeletal muscle corresponds to the length of the thick filaments (myosin) and includes regions of overlap with actin filaments. It is not analogous to dense bodies.

 

Option C. M line: The M line is the central region of the sarcomere in skeletal muscle, where thick filaments (myosin) are held together. This structure is not related to actin filament anchoring and thus is not analogous to dense bodies.

 

Option D. H band: The H band is a zone within the A band where only thick filaments (myosin) are present, with no overlap with actin filaments. It is unrelated to the anchoring of actin filaments or dense bodies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dense bodies in smooth muscle are functionally equivalent to Z lines in skeletal muscle, serving as the anchoring points for actin filaments to facilitate contraction.

questions.stem: A motorcyclist suffered head injury 6 months back and presents with persistent memory deficits following injury. Choose the most appropriately matched option related to memory?
questions.solutionHtml:
;

 

Explanation:

 

Declarative memory (explicit memory) involves the ability to consciously recall facts, events, and information. The medial temporal lobe, which includes the hippocampus, plays a critical role in forming and retrieving declarative memories, particularly episodic memory (personal experiences and events) and semantic memory (facts and general knowledge).

 

In this patient with persistent memory deficits after a head injury, the involvement of the medial temporal lobe would explain difficulties in declarative memory. The hippocampus is a key component in this region and is specifically associated with encoding and retrieval of declarative memory.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hippocampus and implicit memory: The hippocampus is not primarily involved in implicit memory (non-declarative memory, which includes skills and procedural tasks). Implicit memory is mediated by the cerebellum, striatum, and motor cortex, which are responsible for motor learning and procedural memory.

 

Option B. Neocortex and associative learning: The neocortex is involved in priming and perception, not associative learning. Associative learning (conditioning) is governed by the amygdala and cerebellum, making this pairing incorrect.

 

Option D. Angular gyrus - Procedural memory: The angular gyrus is responsible for functions such as word memory, reading, writing, and numbers, not procedural memory. Procedural memory involves the striatum, cerebellum, and motor cortex, which enable skills like riding a bike or typing.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The medial temporal lobe, particularly the hippocampus, is essential for declarative memory (explicit memory) involving facts and personal events. Damage to this region can result in significant deficits in memory formation and recall, as seen in this patient.

questions.stem: Which one of the following clinical disorder specifically arises due to the defective functioning of aquaporins, notably AQP2, crucial for water reabsorption in the kidney tubules, which disrupts the kidney's ability to concentrate urine, resulting in an excessive urine output, thirst, and potential dehydration despite adequate fluid intake.
questions.solutionHtml:
genic DI

 

Explanation:

 

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI) arises due to a defect in the functioning of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) channels in the collecting ducts of the kidney. These channels are critical for water reabsorption in response to antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also called vasopressin).

 

In nephrogenic DI:

 

  • ADH is produced normally, but the kidney's response to ADH is impaired due to defective AQP2 or its signaling pathway.
  • This leads to reduced water reabsorption, resulting in the excretion of large amounts of dilute urine, excessive thirst (polydipsia), and potential dehydration despite normal or increased fluid intake.

 

The distinction between central and nephrogenic DI:

 

  • In central DI, ADH production is impaired, typically due to damage to the hypothalamus or pituitary gland.
  • In nephrogenic DI, ADH production is normal, but the kidneys fail to respond due to defective AQP2 or associated pathways.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Liddle syndrome: Liddle syndrome involves a gain-of-function mutation in the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), leading to excessive sodium reabsorption, hypertension, and hypokalemia. It is unrelated to AQP2 or water reabsorption.

 

Option C. Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is a genetic condition associated with the development of tumors and cysts in various organs, including kidneys. While it may involve kidney dysfunction, it is unrelated to AQP2 or nephrogenic DI.

 

Option D. Bartter syndrome: Bartter syndrome is a group of disorders characterized by defective reabsorption of sodium, potassium, and chloride in the loop of Henle. It leads to hypokalemia, alkalosis, and polyuria, but it is not caused by a defect in aquaporins or ADH pathways.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Nephrogenic DI occurs due to defective functioning of AQP2 channels, impairing water reabsorption in the kidneys despite normal ADH production, leading to excessive urine output and potential dehydration.

questions.stem: Many signalling pathways involve the generation of inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG). These molecules:
questions.solutionHtml:
2 

 

Explanation:

 

IP3 (inositol trisphosphate) and DAG (diacylglycerol) are secondary messengers formed when the enzyme phospholipase C (PLC) cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), a phospholipid present in the cell membrane.

 

  • IP3: Water-soluble and diffuses into the cytoplasm to bind to receptors on the endoplasmic reticulum, causing the release of calcium ions (Ca²⁺).
  • DAG: Lipid-soluble and remains in the membrane, where it activates protein kinase C (PKC) to mediate further signaling.

 

These secondary messengers are critical in several signaling pathways, including those triggered by G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and some tyrosine kinase receptors.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Are first messengers: First messengers are extracellular signaling molecules like hormones, neurotransmitters, or growth factors that bind to receptors. IP3 and DAG are secondary messengers, not first messengers.

 

Option B. Activate phospholipase C: IP3 and DAG are not responsible for activating phospholipase C; instead, they are formed by the action of phospholipase C on PIP2.

 

Option C. Can activate tyrosine kinase receptors: IP3 and DAG are intracellular messengers that do not directly activate tyrosine kinase receptors. Tyrosine kinase receptors are activated by extracellular ligands, leading to signaling cascades that may involve the generation of IP3 and DAG.

 

Educational Objective:

 

IP3 and DAG are secondary messengers derived from the cleavage of PIP2 by phospholipase C. They play critical roles in intracellular signaling by mediating calcium release (IP3) and activating protein kinase C (DAG).

questions.stem: Which characteristic physiological response pattern is associated with a pulmonary reflex mechanism stimulated by the activation of pulmonary J-receptors, specifically related to the release of inflammatory mediators or pulmonary congestion in conditions such as pulmonary edema or interstitial lung disease? ​​​​​​​
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Pulmonary J-receptors (Juxtacapillary receptors) are specialized sensory receptors located in the alveolar walls near the pulmonary capillaries. These receptors are stimulated by pulmonary congestion, edema, or the release of inflammatory mediators, as seen in conditions like pulmonary edema or interstitial lung disease.

 

Upon activation, J-receptors trigger a reflex mediated by the vagus nerve (a parasympathetic response), which results in:

 

  • Slow breathing (bradypnea): This is the initial effect caused by the inhibition of respiratory centers.
  • Bradycardia: A result of vagal stimulation leading to decreased heart rate.
  • Hypotension: Vagal activation reduces sympathetic tone, leading to vasodilation and a drop in blood pressure.

 

This triad is a hallmark of the J-receptor reflex and is also referred to as the pulmonary C-fiber reflex or a variation of the Jarisch reflex, depending on the context.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rapid breathing, tachycardia, hypotension: While peripheral chemoreceptors (in hypoxia) or irritant receptors could lead to rapid breathing (tachypnea), this is not characteristic of the pulmonary J-receptor reflex. J-receptor activation primarily induces bradypnea, not tachypnea.

 

Option B. Slow breathing, tachycardia, hypertension: Although J-receptor activation leads to slow breathing, it does not cause tachycardia or hypertension. The vagus-mediated response decreases both heart rate (bradycardia) and blood pressure (hypotension).

 

Option C. Rapid breathing, bradycardia, hypertension: This combination does not align with the reflex mechanism of J-receptors. Rapid breathing is not part of the initial response, and hypertension is not associated with J-receptor stimulation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The J-receptor reflex induced by pulmonary congestion or edema results in slow breathing (bradypnea), bradycardia, and hypotension, mediated via the vagus nerve. This is a parasympathetic response to pulmonary stress.

questions.stem: All the following are properties of ventricular muscle fibers: All or none lawLength tension relationTetanus Long refractory period
questions.solutionHtml:
1, 2 and 4

 

Explanation:

 

Ventricular muscle fibers possess several unique physiological properties, which are as follows:

 

1. All or None Law: Ventricular muscle fibers act as a functional syncytium due to the presence of gap junctions. This ensures that either all the fibers contract together or none contract, enabling effective pumping of blood.

 

2. Length-Tension Relation: The length-tension relationship in ventricular muscle fibers is analogous to the Frank-Starling law, where an increase in initial fiber length (preload) leads to increased tension (stroke volume). This mechanism allows the heart to adapt to varying volumes of venous return.

 

4. Long Refractory Period: Ventricular muscle fibers have a prolonged refractory period, which ensures that each contraction is followed by adequate relaxation before the next contraction. This property is crucial for maintaining rhythmic and effective cardiac function.

 

Other Option:

 

3. Tetanus: Tetanus does not occur in ventricular muscle fibers. This is due to the long refractory period of cardiac muscle, which prevents summation of contractions and ensures proper relaxation between beats. If tetanus occurred in the heart, effective pumping would be impossible, leading to severe circulatory failure.

 

Thus, tetanus is not a property of ventricular muscle fibers, making the correct answer 1, 2, and 4 only.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ventricular muscle fibers follow the all or none law, exhibit a length-tension relationship, and have a long refractory period. However, tetanus is absent in cardiac muscle due to the long refractory period, preventing summation of contractions.

questions.stem: Erythropoietin is produced by: Kidney Liver Spleen Lung Select the correct answer given below code:
questions.solutionHtml:
b 

 

Explanation:

 

Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone that plays a crucial role in stimulating red blood cell production (erythropoiesis). Its primary sites of production are:

 

  1. Kidney:
    • The majority of erythropoietin (80–85%) is produced by the interstitial cells of the peritubular capillaries in the kidney.
    • The production of EPO is regulated by oxygen-sensing mechanisms in the kidney. Hypoxia stimulates its secretion.
  2. Liver:
    • About 10–15% of erythropoietin is produced in the liver by perisinusoidal hepatocytes.
    • Liver production of EPO is more prominent during fetal development and decreases significantly after birth, as kidney production becomes the primary source.

 

Note:

 

Other sites such as the spleen, brain, and lungs may express mRNA for erythropoietin, but functional EPO is not actively produced there to contribute to erythropoiesis in humans.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Erythropoietin is produced predominantly in the kidney (80–85%) and, to a lesser extent, in the liver (10–15%). Other organs like the spleen and lungs may express mRNA for erythropoietin but do not contribute functionally to its production.

questions.stem: In the cardiac muscle, the inhibition of Na+ K+ ATPase results in?
questions.solutionHtml:
risation

 

Explanation:

 

The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump plays a critical role in maintaining the resting membrane potential in cardiac muscle cells by actively transporting:

 

  • 3 sodium ions (Na⁺) out of the cell, and
  • 2 potassium ions (K⁺) into the cell.

 

This creates a net negative charge inside the cell relative to the outside, contributing to the resting membrane potential.

 

When the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase is inhibited:

 

  • Sodium ions accumulate inside the cell because they are no longer being transported out.
  • Potassium ions decrease inside the cell because they are no longer being transported in.

 

The resulting accumulation of positive charge inside the cell (due to retained Na⁺) reduces the negative resting potential, leading to depolarisation. This depolarisation makes the cell more excitable, which can have significant effects on cardiac contractility and rhythm.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hyperpolarisation and then Depolarisation: Hyperpolarisation occurs when the inside of the cell becomes more negative, which is the opposite of what happens with Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase inhibition. Thus, this option is incorrect.

 

Option C. Hyperpolarisation: This is incorrect because hyperpolarisation requires the inside of the cell to become more negative, which does not happen when Na⁺ accumulates inside the cell.

 

Option D. Repolarisation: Repolarisation is the process of returning the cell to its resting potential after depolarisation. Inhibition of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase does not directly cause repolarisation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Inhibition of the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase in cardiac muscle leads to depolarisation due to the accumulation of sodium ions inside the cell and the disruption of the electrochemical gradient.

questions.stem: During submandibular gland tumor removal lingual nerve was found to be damaged. Which of the following statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Taste sensation of posterior one-third of tongue is lost.

options.label: B
options.text: Taste sensation of anterior two-third of tongue is lost.

options.label: C
options.text: General sensation of posterior one-third of tongue is lost.

options.label: D
options.text: General sensation of anterior two-third of tongue is lost.

questions.answerText: General sensation of anterior two-third of tongue is lost.
questions.solutionHtml:
">Explanation:

 

The lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), is responsible for providing general sensation (touch, temperature, pain) to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

 

  • If the lingual nerve is damaged during submandibular gland surgery, the patient will lose general sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, meaning they cannot perceive touch, heat, or cold in this region.
  • The taste sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani nerve, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). Since the lingual nerve is unrelated to taste sensation, damage to it does not affect taste perception.

 

 

Key relationships:

 

  • Anterior two-thirds of the tongue:
    • General sensation: Lingual nerve (CN V3)
    • Taste sensation: Chorda tympani (CN VII)
  • Posterior one-third of the tongue:
    • Both general sensation and taste: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
  • Posterior-most part of the tongue:
    • Both general sensation and taste: Vagus nerve (CN X).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Damage to the lingual nerve results in the loss of general sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but it does not affect taste perception in this region, as taste is carried by the chorda tympani (CN VII).

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the AV nodal delay?

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibits the depolarization of the atrial chambers

options.label: C
options.text: Facilitates the atrial contraction ahead of ventricles

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibits the repolarization of the ventricles

questions.answerText: Facilitates the atrial contraction ahead of ventricles
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

The atrioventricular (AV) nodal delay refers to the brief delay in the conduction of electrical impulses from the atria to the ventricles via the AV node. This delay is crucial because it:

 

  1. Allows the atria to contract completely before the ventricles begin to contract.
    • This ensures that blood from the atria is properly ejected into the ventricles before the ventricles depolarize and contract.
  2. Maintains synchrony between atrial and ventricular contractions, optimizing cardiac output by ensuring efficient ventricular filling.

 

The AV nodal delay does not directly affect depolarization or repolarization processes but simply slows the transmission of impulses for a critical physiological purpose.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Promotes the excitation of ventricles: Incorrect. The AV nodal delay does not promote ventricular excitation but temporarily slows down impulse conduction to allow atrial contraction to finish.

 

Option B. Inhibits the depolarization of the atrial chambers: Incorrect. The atrial depolarization occurs before the signal reaches the AV node. The AV nodal delay does not inhibit this process; it simply delays the conduction of impulses to the ventricles.

 

Option D. Inhibits the repolarization of the ventricles: Incorrect. The AV nodal delay does not affect ventricular repolarization. It is limited to delaying the conduction of electrical signals to ensure proper timing of atrial and ventricular contractions.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The AV nodal delay is essential for facilitating the atrial contraction ahead of ventricular contraction, ensuring proper filling of the ventricles and maintaining cardiac efficiency.

questions.stem: The velocity of the blood flow will be the lowest in which part of the circulatory system?
questions.solutionHtml:
llaries

 

Explanation:

 

The velocity of blood flow is lowest in the capillaries due to their high total cross-sectional area. This is a crucial physiological adaptation as it:

 

  1. Allows sufficient time for exchange:
    • Nutrients, oxygen, and waste products are exchanged between the blood and tissues at the capillary level. A slower flow ensures efficient exchange.
  2. Ensures effective diffusion:
    • The slow velocity facilitates the diffusion of gases, nutrients, and metabolic waste across the thin capillary walls.

 

The relationship between velocity, flow, and cross-sectional area is governed by the equation:

 



Where v is velocity, Q is flow, and A is cross-sectional area. The capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional area, resulting in the slowest velocity of blood flow.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Arterioles: Arterioles have a smaller cross-sectional area compared to capillaries. Blood flow is slower than in larger vessels like arteries but faster than in capillaries.

 

Option C. Venules: Venules are larger than capillaries and have a smaller total cross-sectional area, so the velocity of blood flow is faster than in capillaries.

 

Option D. Veins: Veins carry blood back to the heart. The total cross-sectional area of veins is much smaller than that of capillaries, resulting in a higher velocity of blood flow.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The velocity of blood flow is lowest in the capillaries to facilitate the efficient exchange of nutrients, gases, and waste between the blood and tissues.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be used in the measurement of cerebral blood flow?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Nitrous oxide

 

Nitrous oxide can be used to measure cerebral blood flow. The method used is called as Kety’s method. 

 

The blood flow of any organ can be measured by determining the amount of a given substance (Qx) removed from the bloodstream by the organ per unit of time and dividing that value by the dif­ference between the concentration of the substance in arterial blood and the concentration in the venous blood from the organ ([Ax] – [Vx]). Thus,

 

 

  • The cerebral blood flow can be defined as the volume of blood flow in the brain tissue in unit time (usually expressed as mL of blood per 100 of tissue per minute)
  • In young adults, the average cerebral blood flow will be 54 mL/100g/min and the blood flow for the entire brain will be around 756 mL/min
  • The inhaled nitrous oxide (N2O) can be used in the clinical measurement of the cerebral blood flow

The Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity used to predict the flow characteristics of a fluid, specifically whether the flow will be laminar or turbulent. It is calculated using the formula:

questions.stem: Which of the following are true about the pulmonary circulation? Low pressureLow flowHigh resistanceHigh compliance
questions.solutionHtml:
font-size:14.0pt;">The pulmonary circulation has distinct physiological characteristics to accommodate the function of oxygenation in the lungs. These features include:

 

  1. Low Pressure:
    • Pulmonary circulation operates at a much lower pressure compared to systemic circulation to prevent damage to the delicate alveolar-capillary interface.
    • Right ventricular output is delivered at lower pressures because the pulmonary vessels are thin-walled and less muscular.
  2. High Compliance:
    • Pulmonary vessels are highly compliant, meaning they can accommodate large increases in blood volume without a significant rise in pressure.
    • This is critical to handle the blood flow from the right ventricle without causing pulmonary edema.
  3. Low Resistance:
    • Pulmonary circulation has low resistance compared to systemic circulation, which ensures efficient blood flow for gas exchange.
  4. Normal Flow (Not Low Flow):
    • The pulmonary circulation has a flow that matches the cardiac output from the right ventricle. It is not low flow, as this would impair gas exchange.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pulmonary circulation is characterized by low pressure and high compliance, allowing it to accommodate the blood output from the right ventricle efficiently while maintaining optimal conditions for gas exchange.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of controlled hypertension is undergoing an echocardiographic evaluation as part of his routine follow-up. The echo reveals an end-systolic volume (ESV) of 70 mL and an end-diastolic volume (EDV) of 130 mL. His resting cardiac output, measured by thermodilution during the same procedure, is reported as 5 L/min. What is this patient's stroke volume?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

The stroke volume (SV) is calculated using the formula:

 

SV=EDV−ESV

 

Where:

 

  • EDV (End-Diastolic Volume): The volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole (130 mL).
  • ESV (End-Systolic Volume): The volume of blood remaining in the ventricle after systole (70 mL).

 

SV=130 mL−70 mL=60 mL

 

The cardiac output (CO) is unnecessary for this calculation as it is not used in the direct determination of stroke volume.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Stroke Volume (SV) is calculated by subtracting the End-Systolic Volume (ESV) from the End-Diastolic Volume (EDV). For this patient, the stroke volume is 60 mL.

  • Assertion Analysis: The assertion that the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by specialized gap junctions is incorrect.
